title: Final Exam & Certificate
goal: Show you can combine shortcuts, formulas, lookups, dynamic arrays and good judgement about pivots, cleaning and AI across the whole course.

steps.prompt: You're on the first sale, ==C2==. Select every sale down to the last row without touching the mouse.
clues: Use the shortcut that selects as it jumps to the end of the data.

steps.prompt: The manager only wants **Q1 and Q3** sales, across all three stores. Put that combined total in ==B5==.
steps.explain: **610**: Q1 is 300 and Q3 is 310. One SUM took both columns, with a comma between the two ranges, and skipped Q2 and Q4.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Add up the numbers with SUM.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only the Q1 column and the Q3 column for the three stores, not Q2 or Q4.

clues: Two ranges can live in one function, separated by a comma.

steps.prompt: You're in the Price column. Put the most expensive item at the top, keeping every row together. (On a Mac, use the Sort button on the Data tab.)
Five colleagues split the lunch bill. In ==B8==, show **Dev's share** of the total as a decimal rounded to **3 places**.
steps.explain: **0.165**: Dev's 380 out of a 2300 total is 0.16521…, and rounding to 3 places leaves 0.165. Without ROUND you'd see a long, untidy decimal.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: The answer must be rounded to 3 decimal places.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Dev's bill divided by the **whole** total, then rounded to 3 places: three digits after the point.

steps.prompt: Reps earn a **1000** bonus when their sales are **at least 5000** and their rating is **at least 4**. Otherwise they get nothing. Work out Meera's bonus in ==D2==.
steps.explain: **1000**: Meera sits exactly on both limits, and “at least” counts the limit itself. Using `>` instead of `>=` would have wrongly sent her home with 0.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: A decision with two conditions that must both be true.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Meera's numbers are exactly on the limits. “At least” includes the limit itself.

steps.prompt: How many orders from **Delhi** were worth **500 or more**? Answer in ==E2==.
steps.explain: **3**: Delhi's 800, 500 and 1200. Delhi has 4 orders and the whole list has 5 orders of 500+, so both conditions were needed.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Count rows that meet two conditions at once.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Delhi **and** 500 or more. Remember an order of exactly 500 counts.

clues: One pair of range and condition for the city, another for the amount.

steps.prompt: Every staff ID ends with the city name. In ==B2==, show just the city from the ID in `A2`.
steps.explain: **Mumbai**: the city is whatever follows the second dash. Taking a fixed number of characters from the right would work for `Pune` but break for `Mumbai`.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only the city name, with nothing else: no code and no dashes.

steps.prompt: An order was placed on Monday 5 January and is due on Tuesday 20 January. How many **working days** (Monday to Friday) is that, counting both days? Answer in ==C2==.
steps.explain: **12**: the 16 calendar days contain two full weekends (4 days), leaving 12 working days. Subtracting the dates would have said 15.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Excel has a function that skips Saturdays and Sundays for you.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Weekends don't count, and both the first and last day are included.

clues: Look for a function with “workdays” in its name.

steps.prompt: The customer asked for the item in `D2`. In ==E2==, show its price from the list, or the words **Not stocked** if it isn't on the list.
steps.explain: **Not stocked**: Pastry isn't in the list, so instead of `#N/A` the lookup returned your own message. Change `D2` to Cake and the same formula gives 120.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use a lookup, and give it a message to show when nothing is found.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Look up the item typed in `D2`, don't type the word yourself.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Pastry isn't on the list, so the cell should show the words **Not stocked**.

clues: The lookup's fourth argument is what to show when nothing matches.

steps.prompt: Find the sales for the product in `B6` in the month in `B7`. Answer in ==B8==, with a formula that still works if either choice changes.
steps.explain: **110**: Coffee is the 2nd row and Feb the 2nd column of the table, and INDEX returned the cell where they cross. Change `B6` or `B7` and it follows.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: A two-way lookup: find the row, find the column, then fetch the cell where they cross.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Use the product in `B6` and the month in `B7`, not typed words.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Coffee's row and Feb's column cross at one cell: 110.

steps.prompt:
A conditional-formatting rule applied to `A2:C5` is:

`=AND($C2="No",$B2<$F$1)`

`F1` holds today's date. Select the cells that turn red.
steps.wrongFeedback: Only invoice 103 is unpaid **and** due before 15 March. Invoice 101 is paid, 102 is due today (not before it) and 104 isn't due yet.
clues: Both parts of the AND must be true for a row. Check the dates carefully.

steps.prompt: A PivotTable is built from this data: Region down the side, Month across the top, **Sum of Sales** in the middle. What number will it show for **West** in **Feb**? Answer in ==E2==.
steps.explain: **500**: West has two Feb rows, 300 and 200, and a pivot adds up every row in a cell. Feb across all regions would be 950 and all of West would be 1150.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: A pivot adds up every row that fits both the row and column label.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: West **and** Feb, adding every matching row, not just the first.

clues: Sum the Sales where Region is West and Month is Feb.

steps.prompt: With **one** formula starting in ==E2==, list the names of everyone in **Pune** who scored **70 or more**.
steps.explain: **Asha, Chitra and Farhan** spilled down `E2:E4`. Chitra scored exactly 70, so `>=` keeps her; Dev is in Pune but scored 64, and Ben scored 91 in Delhi.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: You want a **list** of names that meet two conditions, from one formula.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Pune **and** a score of 70 or more (70 counts). The list should be three names.

clues: Multiply two tests together to require both.

steps.prompt:
A messy export arrives from the same system every month: same columns, different rows. You clean it by hand each time (trim names, fix dates, delete blank rows) and it takes 40 minutes.

What's the best way to save that time?
options: Record the steps in Power Query
steps.explain: Power Query records each cleaning step once. Next month you drop in the new file and click **Refresh**, and every step replays on the new rows. Flash Fill works one column at a time and doesn't re-run itself.
wrongFeedback: Overtyping means re-doing the cleaning and risks mixing old and new numbers.
Flash Fill guesses a pattern for one column, and you'd have to repeat it every month.
clues: Which tool remembers a whole list of steps?

steps.prompt:
You ask an AI assistant for the total sales of Pune, and it says **12,450**. It didn't explain how it got that. You're about to put the number in a report.

What's the smartest next step?
options: Use it: the AI saw the data
Check it with your own SUMIFS
Ask the AI if it's sure
steps.explain: AI answers can sound confident and still be wrong, so confirm with something you control: your own formula, or adding a few rows by hand. Also keep private customer details out of public chatbots in the first place.
wrongFeedback: The AI may have misread the data or guessed. Never put an unchecked number in a report.
The AI will usually say yes. Asking it to grade its own answer isn't a real check.
clues: How could you get the same number without the AI?
